strengths: Introduces a coherent framing of LLM evaluation as set-valued hypothesis generation under underdetermination, with three metrics (Validity, Uniqueness, Recovery) that cleanly operationalize appropriateness, originality, and fluency from creativity theory.

The use of deterministic validators and exactly enumerated admissible sets H_O is a genuine methodological strength: it avoids LLM-as-judge circularity and enables objective, model-agnostic coverage measurement.

Three structurally distinct domains (causal DAGs, gravity-constrained voxels, Boolean genetic programs) with controllable difficulty knobs is a reasonable design for probing complementary reasoning skills.
Broad evaluation across seven current models, including reasoning and instruction-tuned families, with a transparent cost/token accounting in Appendix A.
weaknesses: The central claim that 'even frontier reasoning models exhibit pronounced mode collapse' is contradicted by the authors' own Table 1: GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4 attain 100% VR/NR/RR on Causal and near-100% on 3D across all difficulties. These tasks are saturated for the strongest models, so they are not discriminative, and the headline finding reduces to 'some models collapse,' not the claimed general result.

The repeated assertion that 'reasoning models consistently beat non-reasoning baselines on VR' and that non-reasoning models show 'degraded VR' is directly contradicted in Task 3 (DNA): at difficulty 2, gpt-4o has VR 83.0% and llama-3.3 has 55.8%, while gpt-5 has 74.9% and gemini-2.5-pro 72.3%; at difficulty 3, gpt-4o (68.1%) and llama (66.8%) again exceed gpt-5 (65.1%). The evidence does not support the stated conclusion.

|H_O| — the paper's central independent variable — is never reported for any setting. Difficulty is described only by labels (nodes=4/5/6, tp=1/2/3, basic/extended/full), so readers cannot verify the claim that performance degrades as |H_O| grows, nor assess controllability, which the paper lists as a required property (Section 3).

The sampling protocol sets N = |H_O| and draws N 'independent' samples, which makes Recovery and ceiling behavior ambiguous (perfect RR requires exactly one distinct valid sample per hypothesis) and conflates sampling budget with target size. No justification or sensitivity analysis is given for this choice, despite the paper noting 'other sampling budgets are possible.'

Reproducibility is insufficient: the text states 'Full prompts and decoding settings are provided in our repository' but no repository link is given, and the actual instances, prompts, enumeration procedure, and canonicalizer implementation are not provided. The exact tasks (specific DAGs, projections, Boolean targets) cannot be reconstructed.

The optional 'Divergent-creativity view' (Section 3.2) introduces a posterior plausibility P(h_i|O) and C_count/C_entropy but never specifies how the posterior is computed or connects it to VR/NR/RR. Similarly, Section 3.3 concedes 'our diagnostics do not directly estimate entropies,' yet Figure 3 plots 'cumulative entropy' without defining the underlying distribution, and the '0.5 vertical offset for visual clarity' is unexplained. These analyses are underspecified and add confusion rather than evidence.

Several numerical patterns are unexplained and untested: NR equals RR exactly in many rows (e.g., gpt-4o and claude-opus-4 at DNA difficulty 1), which requires justification given VR<100%, and the statistics are thin (number of repeated runs unspecified, standard deviations reaching ~45%, no significance testing for the cross-model comparisons).

The Boolean canonicalizer collapses only commutativity, idempotence, and associativity, so many semantically equivalent expressions are counted as distinct. This inflates |H_O| and makes the 'coverage' interpretation of Recovery partly an artifact of the restricted canonicalizer, which the paper acknowledges but does not quantify.

The novelty claim ('to the best of our knowledge, this is the very first exploration in this direction') is overstated relative to the creativity/diversity benchmarks the authors themselves cite (HypoBench, IdeaBench, CreativEval, LiveIdeaBench), which also evaluate non-redundant multi-hypothesis generation; the specific added value is the exact enumeration, which should be framed as the contribution rather than 'first exploration.'
Grouping LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct with GPT-4o as 'non-reasoning' conflates reasoning mode with overall capability and model vintage, so the reasoning-vs-non-reasoning contrast is confounded.

The causal forward model (intervention on node i sets all non-descendants to 0 and descendants to 1) is highly restrictive, so the mapping to genuine 'scientific underdetermination' is asserted rather than demonstrated; the domains remain toy settings whose relevance to real scientific inference is unclear.

strengths: The problem framing—evaluating LLMs as set-valued hypothesis generators under underdetermination—is well-motivated and genuinely relevant to scientific reasoning, where multiple mechanistically distinct explanations can fit the same data.

Using deterministic, task-specific validators together with exactly enumerated admissible sets (H_O) is a sound design choice that avoids the circularity and subjectivity of LLM-as-judge or human-rater creativity evaluations.

The three instantiated domains (causal DAGs from perturbations, gravity-constrained 3D voxel reconstruction, Boolean genetic interactions) span structural, spatial, and symbolic reasoning and provide controllable difficulty knobs that plausibly vary |H_O|.
The paper is reasonably honest about scope, explicitly stating it is a controlled probe rather than a leaderboard and not a claim about real-world scientific discovery.
The empirical study is broad, covering seven recent frontier and open models with a cost/token accounting appendix.
weaknesses: Missing a trivial uniform-random baseline. Since N = |H_O| samples are drawn and RR measures coverage of H_O, a uniform sampler would cover only ~1-(1-1/|H_O|)^|H_O| ≈ 63% of the space by the coupon-collector effect. Without this reference point, the central 'mode collapse' finding is not interpretable: degraded RR may simply reflect the inherent difficulty of covering a finite space with N samples rather than any model-specific collapse. This is a decisive evidential gap for the paper's main claim.

RR is mechanically bounded by VR (RR = |valid ∧ novel|/|H_O| ≤ |valid|/|H_O| = VR when N = |H_O|), so any VR drop forces an RR drop. The abstract and narrative claim that 'Validity often remains high while Uniqueness and Recovery degrade,' but in the paper's own most discriminative task (Boolean genetic interactions, Table 1) VR collapses alongside RR (e.g., GPT-5 VR 74.9%→65.1%, Claude-Opus-4 52.7%→38.9%, GPT-4o 83.0%→68.1%). The headline claim is therefore contradicted by the strongest evidence in the paper, and the 'collapse' is at least partly a validity failure rather than a coverage failure.

NR is frequently identical to VR in the tables (e.g., GPT-5 causal D1: VR=NR=RR=100%; GPT-5 DNA extended: VR=NR=74.9%; Gemini-2.5-Pro DNA D3: VR=52.2% vs NR=48.9%). This indicates the non-redundancy signal is largely redundant with validity and adds little independent diagnostic information; the three-metric decomposition is not as informative as claimed.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code repository URL is given despite 'Full prompts and decoding settings are provided in our repository'; prompts, schemas, and instance configurations are not included in the manuscript, and Table 1 only exposes minimal knobs (e.g., 'nodes=4', 'tp=1'). The exact hypothesis-space enumeration and canonicalizer code are essential to the claims and are unavailable.

Results carry very large variance (std up to ±40% in several cells), yet the paper makes strong comparative claims about model families (reasoning vs. non-reasoning). With such dispersion and unclear numbers of repeated runs/instances, the ranking and 'reasoning helps' conclusions are not statistically supported (no significance tests, no per-instance detail).

The information-theoretic analysis (Sec. 3.3, 5.5, Fig. 3) is underdeveloped and unclear: the stepwise entropy definition over a growing multiset M_t is not well-posed (entropy of an ever-growing empirical distribution is not a meaningful information gain), the caption/text is vague, and a '0.5 vertical offset for visual clarity' obscures the actual scale. This analysis does not provide the mechanistic evidence it is claimed to.

The contribution is presented as 'the very first exploration in this direction,' an overclaim given closely related work the authors themselves cite (HypoBench, IdeaBench, LiveIdeaBench, Nagarajan et al. on diversity/originality). The novelty is incremental relative to existing diversity/coverage-style evaluations.

Presentation issues: model names are garbled ('flama-3.3-70b-instruct', 'gemini-2.5-pes', 'gemini-2'), the reference list has duplicated/restarting numbering, and Table 1 is dense and hard to parse. Figure images appear broken in the provided file, limiting assessment of Figures 3 and 4.

The design choice N = |H_O| is questionable for coverage analysis: to estimate coverage of a set of size |H_O|, the number of samples should scale well beyond |H_O|, and the paper never justifies why this budget is appropriate or how results change with different budgets (it merely asserts 'other sampling budgets are possible').

strengths: Introduces a useful diagnostic suite for set-valued hypothesis generation under underdetermination, moving beyond single-answer correctness.
The VR/NR/RR metrics are simple, interpretable, and grounded in creativity theory, with deterministic validators and exactly enumerated admissible sets that avoid LLM-as-judge circularity.
The three task domains (causal graphs, 3D voxel reconstruction under gravity, Boolean genetic interactions) are diverse and expose controllable difficulty knobs.
The empirical evaluation spans recent frontier and non-reasoning models and reveals mode-collapse patterns that correctness-only metrics would miss.
The paper is generally well-written, with clear figures, model metadata, cost/token analysis, and an honest scope statement that it is a controlled diagnostic rather than a leaderboard.
weaknesses: The sampling protocol is ambiguous and internally inconsistent: the paper says it draws 'N independent samples,' but the task sections condition generation on the history A_h. If history is provided, the task is sequential enumeration rather than independent sampling, which changes the interpretation of all VR/NR/RR results.

The paper sets N = |H_O| in most experiments. If samples were truly independent, 100% RR would be statistically implausible for most hypothesis spaces; the near-100% RR results strongly suggest history-conditioned generation, which the paper does not clearly acknowledge or analyze.

The manuscript does not report |H_O| values for most settings. Since the central claim is that Uniqueness and Recovery degrade as |H_O| grows, the absence of this table prevents verification of the scaling relationship and weakens the main empirical argument.

The Boolean canonicalizer collapses only local algebraic symmetries (commutativity, idempotence, associativity flattening). Functionally equivalent expressions under distributivity, De Morgan, absorption, etc. may be counted as distinct hypotheses, potentially distorting NR/RR and overstating mode collapse for the Boolean task.

NR is not conditioned on validity, so high NR can reflect diverse invalid proposals rather than genuine exploration. For example, LLaMA on causal inference (nodes=4) has VR 30.0% but NR 83.3%, undermining the blanket claim that Uniqueness degrades with |H_O|.
The information-theoretic analysis in Section 3.3 and Figure 3 is under-specified: the pattern map M_t is not defined, so the entropy/information-gain quantities are hard to interpret or reproduce.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no repository link or full prompts/decoding settings are provided in the manuscript, the number of instances per condition and whether runs were repeated are unclear, and standard deviations are described inconsistently across instances vs. repeated runs.

The paper overclaims novelty ('very first exploration in this direction') despite related work on hypothesis-generation and creativity benchmarks such as HypoBench, IdeaBench, CreativEval, and LiveIdeaBench.
Experimental confounds are not controlled: reasoning models use much larger token budgets (Table 2), so reasoning-vs-non-reasoning comparisons may partly reflect compute rather than capability.

Several results contradict the narrative: in Boolean 'full', GPT-4o and LLaMA have higher VR than several reasoning models, yet the text repeatedly states that reasoning models maintain high performance across all metrics.

Table 1 contains model-name typos ('gemini-2.5-pes', 'flama-3.3-70b-instruct'), and some claims in Section 5.4 (e.g., duplicates as the dominant failure mode) are not universally supported by the table, where invalid generations dominate for GPT-4o on hard 3D settings.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: evaluating whether LLMs can generate multiple distinct valid hypotheses under underdetermination, rather than only single-answer correctness.
The proposed Validity, Uniqueness, and Recovery metrics are simple, interpretable, and use deterministic validators plus exact enumeration to avoid LLM-as-judge subjectivity.

The three domains (causal DAGs, gravity-constrained 3D voxels, Boolean genetic programs) are diverse and expose controllable difficulty knobs, making the suite a potentially reusable diagnostic probe.

The real-world yeast case study, although small, attempts to anchor the synthetic framework in biological data and illustrates how the admissible hypothesis set contracts as additional experiments are added.
The theoretical section gives an intuitive coupon-collector-style explanation for why a peaked generator can maintain high Validity yet recover only a small fraction of the admissible set.
The paper includes a training-free complexity-stratified decoding baseline and reports its mixed effects, showing some improvement in complex-hypothesis recovery for several models.
The manuscript is generally transparent about scope, explicitly stating that it is not a leaderboard and does not claim real-world scientific discovery, and it includes an impact statement.
The appendix adds useful analyses (cost, model preferences, reasoning traces, failure decomposition) that support the diagnostic intent.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated: the abstract and introduction claim a "consistent failure mode: high Validity but sharp degradation in Uniqueness and Recovery" for frontier LLMs, but GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4 achieve 100% or near-100% Recovery on Causal and 3D tasks; in Boolean hard, Validity itself drops (e.g., GPT-5 VR 65.1%, RR 48.0%). The real-world study shows GPT-5 and Grok-4 at 100% RR, directly contradicting the abstract's claim that LLMs exhibit the same mode collapse on real-world data.

The paper repeatedly refers to difficulty scaling via |H_O| but does not report |H_O| for the causal or Boolean tasks (only 3D tp=3 gives |H_O|=27). Without these sizes, readers cannot judge whether the benchmark is challenging or whether the "hard" hypothesis spaces are actually small.

The Boolean distinctness criterion is problematic: the mechanistic canonicalizer collapses only local algebraic symmetries (commutativity, idempotence, associativity flattening). Many Boolean expressions are semantically equivalent under absorption, distributivity, De Morgan, etc., so |H_O| may contain duplicate functions, inflating NR and RR and undermining the claim of exactly enumerated valid hypothesis sets.

The 3D task description is ambiguous: Section 5.2 defines the observation as a single top-down projection, but Section 7.1 and Table 2 use "tp=1,2,3" and "number of top-down views" without defining tp or explaining how multiple views are generated and enumerated.

The real-world study is too small and inconsistent: it uses one anonymized 6-gene module with 13 observations, and the mapping from six genes to the Boolean program space is not described. It cannot support broad claims about real-world underdetermination, and its results contradict the claimed universal mode collapse.

The theoretical contribution is thin and overclaimed: the analysis is standard expected-coverage/coupon-collector reasoning, not a rigorous "sublinear coverage bound." It assumes a fixed peaked distribution p but does not estimate p, alpha, K, or tail mass from the LLMs, nor validate the bound empirically. The title's "sublinear coverage bounds" is not delivered.

The stratified decoding method uses the ground-truth complexity distribution to allocate query budget, which is unavailable in realistic underdetermined settings. It is therefore not a practical mitigation, and its benefits are mixed: it hurts GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1.

Missing experimental details: temperature/top-p, exact prompts, parsing rules, number of instances per difficulty, number of repeated runs, handling of parse failures, and how N=|H_O| is set per instance are not in the manuscript. Saying that full details are in an anonymous repository does not make the manuscript self-contained for reproducibility.

Statistical reporting is weak: means and standard deviations are given without sample sizes, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several standard deviations exceed 40%, suggesting very few instances; claims of "consistent" degradation are not statistically supported.

Uniqueness can be misleading: NR counts novel proposals regardless of validity, so models with 0% VR can have high NR (e.g., Claude and LLaMA in Table 5). The main tables do not isolate diversity among valid hypotheses, so high NR does not necessarily indicate useful exploration.

The paper does not compare stratified decoding against existing diversity-promoting decoding methods (e.g., temperature/top-p tuning, memory-based rejection sampling, novelty search, or self-consistency with diversity objectives), so the conclusion that reshaping the sampling distribution is promising is weakly supported.

The causal task is a restricted abstraction: validity is defined by matching descendant sets under single-node perturbations, which is not the same as standard causal DAG inference. The paper does not discuss how this abstraction limits relevance to causal discovery under underdetermination.

Presentation and consistency issues abound: broken equations, inconsistent terminology (VR/NR/RR vs Validity/Uniqueness/Recovery), undefined "tp", overclaiming "sublinear", and table formatting problems make the paper harder to follow and reduce confidence.

The novelty claim is not fully substantiated: the paper claims to be the "first systematic framework" for set-valued inference under underdetermination, but it does not sufficiently differentiate its contribution from existing diversity/coverage benchmarks such as HypoBench, IdeaBench, CreativEval, and LiveIdeaBench beyond the use of deterministic validators.

The limitations discussion is incomplete: the manuscript does not adequately discuss the restricted Boolean canonicalizer, small hypothesis-space sizes, model saturation on two tasks, prompt/decoding sensitivity, or the use of ground truth in stratified decoding. The impact statement addresses ethics but not these scientific limitations.

Benchmark utility is limited by saturation: if frontier models already achieve near-perfect RR on two of three domains and the hardest domain also shows validity collapse, the suite may not discriminate among current frontier models or provide a clear signal for improvement.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: set-valued hypothesis generation under underdetermination, moving beyond single-answer correctness benchmarks.
Introduces clear, interpretable metrics (Validity, Uniqueness/Novelty, Recovery) that separate consistency from coverage and non-redundancy.

Proposes three structured diagnostic domains (causal DAG inference, 3D voxel reconstruction under gravity, Boolean genetic interactions) with deterministic validators and controllable difficulty knobs, enabling exact validity checks in principle.

Evaluates a broad suite of frontier and non-reasoning LLMs across multiple difficulty levels and reports a consistent mode-collapse pattern: high Validity but degraded Uniqueness and Recovery as task difficulty increases.

Includes a real-world anchoring attempt on yeast genetic interaction data, showing that many Boolean hypotheses remain consistent with observations and that additional double-KO measurements contract the hypothesis space.
Provides a simple training-free mitigation baseline (complexity-stratified decoding) and reports partial improvements for several models.

Reproducibility is partially supported by model version metadata, an anonymous code/prompt repository, and an impact/limitations statement that acknowledges the controlled, non-real-world-discovery setting.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is overstated and elementary. Section 4 derives a standard tail/union bound for coupon-collector-like coverage; the title's 'sublinear coverage bounds' is not substantiated by new theory, and the claimed exponential sampling requirement is heuristic rather than rigorously proven for the benchmark tasks.

The central empirical claim that performance degrades as |H_O| grows is not verifiable from the main paper because |H_O| values are never reported in Tables 1-3. The difficulty knobs (nodes=4/5/6, tp=1/2/3, basic/extended/full) are not sufficient to assess hypothesis-space size, so the scaling story is under-evidenced.

The Boolean canonicalizer only collapses local algebraic symmetries (commutativity, idempotence, associativity flattening). Many logically equivalent Boolean expressions therefore remain distinct in H_O, meaning Recovery may reward enumeration of syntactic variants rather than mechanistically distinct hypotheses. This undermines the interpretation of Boolean task results.

The real-world genetic study is severely underspecified. The hypothesis class used to enumerate 'all Boolean hypotheses' is not defined in the main text, making the enumeration impossible to reproduce or assess. Table 5's NR/RR denominators (e.g., 85.7% = 6/7, 71.4% = 5/7) imply |H_O| or N = 7, which conflicts with Figure 3 showing roughly 20-100 consistent hypotheses and with the stated protocol N = |H_O|.

Experimental results are internally inconsistent. For Boolean hard, Table 3 reports GPT-5 RR = 48.0% and DeepSeek-R1 RR = 36.0%, while Table 4 reports baseline RR = 38.5% and 25.6% for the same models. No explanation is given for these discrepancies, which undermines confidence in the evaluation pipeline.

The stratified decoding baseline uses the ground-truth complexity distribution to allocate the query budget across complexity levels. This is oracle-informed and not a practical training-free decoding method; reported gains may partly reflect access to H_O rather than a generally applicable mitigation.

The sampling protocol is ambiguous and potentially inconsistent: the paper says N independent samples are drawn, but novelty is defined relative to earlier samples and the model is described as generating with history A_h. It is unclear whether the model sees prior proposals, which strongly affects Uniqueness and Recovery. Setting N = |H_O| also couples the sampling budget to ground-truth size, limiting comparability to realistic settings.

The 3D task description is inconsistent. Section 5.2 defines a single top-down projection, but results refer to '3 views' and 'tp=1,2,3'; 'tp' is never defined, and the claim |H_O|=27 for 3 views is not reconciled with the described single-projection hypothesis space.

Metric interpretation is problematic. NR is not conditioned on validity, so high Uniqueness can coexist with zero Validity (as in Table 5). This makes 'Uniqueness' as originality difficult to interpret and weakens the claimed separation of correctness and exploration.

There is little statistical rigor: the number of instances/runs per condition is not clearly reported, no significance tests are provided, and several entries have very large standard deviations (e.g., ±40%), making model comparisons unreliable.

The paper does not adequately analyze whether failures are due to parsing/formatting errors, genuine reasoning limitations, or sampling artifacts in the main text. Some decomposition is deferred to the appendix, but the central claims rely on these unexamined failure modes.

The benchmark tasks are synthetic puzzles with limited connection to real scientific underdetermination. The paper acknowledges this, but the significance for scientific hypothesis generation remains modest, and the 'real-world' study does not compensate because it is not reproducible as described.

Reproducibility is incomplete: decoding parameters, full prompts, and real-world enumeration code are not in the main text; model outputs and instance identifiers are not provided; the anonymized biological module prevents verification of the real-world claims.

Presentation has multiple issues: tables omit key metadata such as |H_O|, figures are low-resolution and some labels are unclear, terminology shifts between 'Novelty' and 'Uniqueness', and several claims are not supported by the reported numbers.

Originality is incremental. Related benchmarks (HypoBench, IdeaBench, CreativEval, LiveIdeaBench) already target diversity/novelty in LLM generation; this paper's main distinction is deterministic validators and enumerated spaces, but the theoretical and methodological advances over prior work are limited.

strengths: Introduces a clear and useful diagnostic formulation of set-valued hypothesis generation under underdetermination, with Validity, Uniqueness, and Recovery metrics that separate correctness from exploration and avoid LLM-as-judge circularity.

Provides three structured domains (causal DAGs, 3D voxel reconstruction under gravity, Boolean genetic interactions) with deterministic validators and exactly enumerable admissible sets, plus a real-world anchored genetic case study.
Reports a broad empirical study across seven LLMs and multiple difficulty levels, with additional analyses of cost, reasoning traces, information-theoretic exploration, and failure modes.

Gives a simple theoretical explanation for why high Validity can coexist with low Recovery when the generator induces a peaked distribution over the admissible set, formalizing an intuitive head-tail argument.
Proposes complexity-stratified decoding as a training-free baseline and shows partial mitigation of coverage collapse on some models.
Reproducibility is supported by model version metadata, reported API costs, and release of prompts/evaluation code in an anonymous repository.
weaknesses: The central claim that frontier LLMs exhibit a 'consistent failure mode' is overstated. Tables 1-2 show GPT-5, Grok-4, and Gemini-2.5-Pro at or near 100% NR/RR in causal inference and 3D reconstruction, so coverage collapse is mainly observed in Boolean genetic interactions and weaker models, not consistently across all frontier LLMs.

The real-world alignment study contradicts the mode-collapse narrative. Table 5 shows GPT-5 and Grok-4 recovering up to 100% of the genetic hypothesis set, while weaker models fail validity (VR=0%), not uniqueness. This does not support the abstract/introduction/conclusion claim that the same mode collapse persists on real-world genetic data.

The sampling protocol is ambiguous and potentially inconsistent with the theory. Section 3 says N independent samples are drawn from a fixed prompt, but Sections 5-6 describe generation conditioned on history A_h and mention memory-based reject-duplicate decoding. If samples are history-dependent, the i.i.d. analysis in Section 4 does not directly apply, and the interpretation of NR/RR becomes unclear.

The Boolean canonicalizer is incomplete: it collapses only commutativity, idempotence, and associativity flattening, leaving many semantically equivalent Boolean expressions distinct. This inflates |H_O| and depresses RR, undermining the claim that the benchmark measures mechanistically distinct hypotheses in its most discriminative task.

Table 4 baseline RR values are inconsistent with Tables 3 and 8 (e.g., GPT-5 38.5% vs 48.0%; Gemini-2.5-Pro 37.2% vs 47.4%; DeepSeek-R1 25.6% vs 36.0%) without explanation, raising reproducibility and comparability concerns.

The main tables omit exact |H_O| values, the number of instances per difficulty level, and full prompt/decoding details, making the reported mean±std and RR magnitudes difficult to interpret. Difficulty labels alone are insufficient.

The theoretical contribution is elementary and the title's 'Sublinear Coverage Bounds' is misleading: the bound is linear in N and conditional on an idealized i.i.d. peaked sampler rather than a bound on LLM behavior.

The proposed complexity-stratified decoding is only partially effective and highly model-dependent: it improves 4/7 models but substantially degrades GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and especially DeepSeek-R1, so the 'simple fix' framing overstates its practical value.
The real-world validation rests on a single anonymized genetic instance, which is too narrow to support broad claims about real-world underdetermination or model behavior.
